To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the following formalin-resistant monoclonal antibodies (MoAbs) are available: CD1a, CD2, CD3, CD4, CD5, CD7, CD8, CD10, CD11c, CD15, CD20, CD30, CD43, CD45, CD56, CD57, CD68, HLA-DR, kappa and lambda.

the use of monocional antibodies against leucocytic differentiation antigens on paraffin sections has become possible by the availability of a growing number of antibodies against formalin-resistant antigens and that the dermatopathologist should be familiar with the precise distribution of the antigens detected, as well as with their crossreactivities with non-leucocytic structures.

the use of monocloal antibodies against formalin-resistant leukocyte differentiation antigens on routinely processed tissue sections is a powerful tool in the diagnosis of cutaneous lymphoproliferative disorders.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the detection of the CD3 complex, the CD4/CD8 ratio, the CD30 antigen (Ki-1), the CD15 antigen (LeuM1) and the CD68 antigen.
the detection of the most important antigens on paraffin sections and the investigation of their distribution in normal skin and in inflammatory infiltrates.
the development of new diagnostic methods in dermatohistology.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the detection of formaline-resistant leucocyte antigens is possible on formaline-fixed paraffin sections with the following antibodies: CD1a, CD2, CD3, CD4, CD5, CD8, CD10, CD11b, CD11c, CD14, CD15, CD16, CD19, CD20, CD21, CD30, CD34, CD45, CD45RA, CD45RO, CD56, CD57, CD68,
the detection of formaline-resistant leucocyte antigens on paraffin sections is possible, but that this technique is not yet ready for use in routine diagnostic dermatopathology.
the use of antibodies against formalin-resistant leukocyte differentiation antigens has become indispensable in dermatopathology.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are now able to diagnose cutaneous leucocyte infiltrates with a considerably greater reliability than ever before, even in the absence of frozen sections.
formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue sections are the best material to study leucocyte differentiation in the skin.

, with the use of formalin-resistant monoclonal antibodies, the dermatohistopathologist can now perform a reliable diagnosis of cutaneous infiltrates of leucocytes and lymphocytes, even when using paraffin sections.
The main takeaway from our work is that

formalin-resistant monoclonal antibodies can be used to detect leucocytes and their subpopulations in formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue sections, and thus can replace the use of fresh tissue for the diagnosis of leucocytic skin infiltrates.

the use of formalin-resistant antibodies in the routine diagnosis of leucocytic infiltrates will allow the dermatopathologist to reach a more precise diagnosis, to detect the exact type of leucocytosis and to identify the cell types that may be responsible for the disease.
the use of antibodies directed against the CD3 complex (CD3 epsilon chain) and the CD20 molecule (L26) is of great value in routine dermatohistopathological diagnostics.
